en: Abhidhānottaratantra, Chapter 26 [Tibetan & Sanskrit, 29] = Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition = 1138 AD palm-leaf manuscript.
[175.6] [1074] Now I shall fully explain another sādhana of the nine-syllable mantra,
which is accomplished through the gnosis of the syllable *Kṣaḥ* and brings about the destruction of all suffering.
The devourer of the destruction of conceptual construction; equal to space, arisen from emptiness, possessing the expanse of the sky as his enjoyment;
six-faced, twelve-armed, three-eyed, with a distorted countenance.
He stands in the ālīḍha posture, the destroyer of the wicked Māra.
He tramples upon Bhairava with the soles of his feet; Bhairavī stands [upon him].
He is clothed in a tiger skin and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
He wears a crown of skulls and is beautified by a crescent moon.
Trampling upon the Viśvavajra with his matted locks, adorned with the body of the six mudrās,
possessing eight terrifying faces that strike fear even into fear itself;
thereafter, [the faces are] blue, smoky-grey, green, red, and yellow as the fifth.
And the sixth has the form of a donkey, with its face turned upward, truly terrifying.
He has the appearance of being reduced to ashes, yet his color removes all suffering;
he is absorbed in union with the vajra and bell, enjoying the fullness of supreme bliss.
In front of Vajravārāhī is one of the same color, with a boar’s head facing upward;
she is absorbed in non-dual yoga, with disheveled hair and naked,
encircling [the deity] to the height of her knees, overwhelmed by compassionate passion.
She holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, with a garment of Brahmā’s hide draped over her upper body.
She wields a vajra, a trident, a hand-drum, a curved knife, a noose, and a severed head;
she brandishes a sword and a skull, appearing fierce and destroying all suffering.
In the heart is Jñānaḍāka, surrounded by Kākāsyā and the others;
in the center of the eight-spoked wheel, according to the sequence from left to right,
one should assign the locations of the Ḍākinīs, including the cremation grounds and the secondary cremation grounds.
Having assigned the syllables yaṃ, raṃ, laṃ, vaṃ, śaṃ, ṣaṃ, saṃ, and haṃ, and having visualized the wisdom-wheel of the ḍākinīs for seven nights according to the sequence of the four junctions,
one should meditate on it by a riverbank or in cremation grounds; one will certainly attain accomplishment.
Having performed abduction and killing, whatever action is desired by the mind is accomplished;
the circle of ḍākinīs succeeds—there is no need for deliberation here.
She is blue, the color of the palāśa flower, and the fourth is red-yellow.
The four [deities], beginning with Samayadā, have faces of various auspicious colors;
they are red, blue, smoky, and white-faced, most excellent and beautiful.
All are three-eyed and three-faced, with disheveled hair and naked.
The left face has the mouth of a crow, and likewise the right has the mouth of an owl;
the third is that of a dog, and the fourth is that of a boar. Thus, the faces on the left and right possess a fierce form according to this rule.
Likewise, the faces beginning with Yamadāḍhī are on the left and right;
those of the ram, camel, horse, lion, goat, cow, and buffalo,
as well as the other animal faces— all are rendered equal in battle.
Holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, with a noose and a goad in her other hands;
she holds a bell, a ḍamaru drum, and a curved knife, wears a crown of garlands of skulls,
and is adorned with the five mudrās.
Seated upon corpses, with dancing feet and short yet elongated vulvas,
their faces terrifying with protruding fangs, they are overwhelmed by the flavor of compassion;
one should meditate upon them through the process of visualization as the secrets of body, speech, and mind.
HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ—thus [is the mantra] called the Secret; situated in the center of the wheel within the vajra-cloud, it resides in the heart of the Jñāna-Ḍāka.
Then, having beheld the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra) within the wheel of the assembly of ḍākinīs, one should become of one flavor (samarasa) with the offering.
One should recite the mantra according to the ritual rules, remaining concentrated on the syllables.
Having well-restrained the breath through *prāṇāyāma*, one should radiate the gnosis born of the three secrets.
Śrī-Ṣaḍākavajra Āḥ Kṣaḥ Hūṃ! Ḍākinījālasamvara Hūṃ Phaṭ!
One should employ the Praṇava at the beginning and the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* at the end;
this is declared to be the mantra of the Ḍākinī, which bestows the fruit of all desires. This supreme secret must not be given to just anyone.
For seven days, one should meditate on [the deity] as subject to one's will through the state of being mute;
then, before long, the circle of ḍākinīs born from the three secrets will be accomplished for him.
In the *Abhidhānottarottara*, the twenty-sixth chapter: the *Kṣaḍākavajrasādhana* (The Sadhana of Kṣaḍākavajra).
